title: The War That May Have Happened
summary: Hittite texts from the thirteenth century BC refer to Wilusa, widely identified with Ilios/Troy, and to disputes involving western Anatolia. Excavations at Hisarlik reveal several destruction levels, including Troy VIIa around the end of the Bronze Age, but archaeology cannot identify Homer's war or prove that one Greek expedition generated the epics. The poems may preserve distant memories of conflict, geography, and elite culture, heavily reshaped by centuries of performance.

title: The World Ends — Writing Disappears
summary: Around 1200 BC, palace systems across the eastern Mediterranean fractured through a still-debated combination of warfare, migration, political instability, environmental stress, and disrupted trade. Mycenaean administration disappeared and Linear B ceased to be used, but Greek-speaking communities and cultural practices continued; the period was not a total civilisational blank. Heroic traditions could have carried selected memories forward, although no continuous chain from palace records to Homer can be demonstrated.

title: The Bards Remember
summary: The Iliad and Odyssey emerged from a long tradition of performed hexameter poetry. Singers used formulas, type-scenes, and inherited story patterns to compose in performance rather than reciting a single immutable script. The tradition preserved old elements while continually adapting them to later audiences, so the epics combine memories from different periods rather than functioning as straightforward Bronze Age testimony.

title: Writing Returns to Greece
summary: During the eighth century BC, Greek communities adapted a Phoenician consonantal script and used letters for vowels, producing an alphabet well suited to recording Greek speech. Early inscriptions show that writing and hexameter verse developed in close proximity, but scholars disagree about when and why the Homeric poems became texts. The alphabet enabled textualisation; it did not by itself create a single moment when oral poetry became fixed literature.

title: Homer Puts Down the Lyre
summary: The Iliad and Odyssey reached forms recognisable to later audiences during the late eighth or seventh century BC, although their composition, dictation, performance, and textualisation may have unfolded over generations. Ancient tradition attached both poems to Homer, but the poems provide no biography and modern scholarship cannot securely identify one author, two authors, or a precise act of writing. Their surviving scale and coherence reflect both exceptional poetic shaping and a much older oral tradition.

title: Who Was Homer?
summary: Debate over the poems' authorship, unity, and transmission began in antiquity and became the modern 'Homeric Question.' Friedrich August Wolf's Prolegomena ad Homerum (1795) argued that long oral development and later editing had to be considered, though his specific reconstruction did not settle the issue. Scholarship now asks multiple questions—about oral composition, textual growth, performance, and editorial transmission—rather than choosing simply between one genius and a committee.

title: The Tyrant Fixes the Text
summary: Later sources connected Peisistratus or his son Hipparchus with regulated Homeric performance at the Panathenaia. Athenian festival rules probably influenced the poems' performance and textual history, but the famous story that Peisistratus collected scattered lays into a definitive edition is late and widely treated as invention or exaggeration. Standardisation was gradual, with rhapsodes, schools, local texts, and later editors all contributing.

title: Every Greek Child Learns Homer
summary: By the classical period Homer occupied a central place in Greek education, performance, and argument. Pupils encountered Homer in literacy and rhetorical training, while historians, playwrights, and philosophers quoted, reinterpreted, and criticised the poems. Plato's attacks on poetry show Homer's authority, but anecdotes such as Alexander sleeping with an Iliad should be treated as later literary traditions rather than classroom documentation.

title: Alexandria Collects and Edits Homer
summary: Hellenistic scholars at Alexandria, especially Zenodotus, Aristophanes of Byzantium, and Aristarchus, compared manuscripts, marked disputed lines, and wrote extensive commentary on Homer. Their work strongly influenced the text and scholia transmitted later, but it did not erase all variation or create the poems from chaos. The surviving tradition reflects earlier performance and copying, Alexandrian criticism, Roman-era transmission, papyri, and medieval manuscripts together.

title: Alexander and Achilles
summary: Ancient biographies portray Alexander as deeply engaged with Achilles and the Iliad, and report that he honoured heroic sites at Troy. Plutarch, citing earlier tradition, says Alexander carried an edition associated with Aristotle, while the famous dagger-and-pillow detail is difficult to take literally for a long poem written on scrolls. His conquests nevertheless expanded Greek institutions and education across the Hellenistic world, increasing the geographical reach of Homeric culture.

title: Virgil Writes Rome's Homer
summary: Virgil's Aeneid, composed in the late first century BC, deliberately engages with both Homeric epics: its wandering first half recalls the Odyssey, while its Italian war recalls the Iliad. Virgil transformed rather than copied Homer, redirecting heroic narrative toward Roman origins, empire, loss, and duty. The Aeneid became a central mediator through which later Latin and European readers encountered Homeric forms.

title: Byzantine Scholars Keep the Flame
summary: Greek-speaking scholars, teachers, and copyists in the eastern Roman and Byzantine worlds kept Homer in education and repeatedly recopied the poems. Most complete medieval witnesses are Byzantine, while ancient papyri preserve earlier and sometimes variant readings. Western humanists later learned Greek from Byzantine teachers and obtained Greek manuscripts, but survival resulted from a broad copying culture rather than one uninterrupted institutional chain.

title: Dante Meets a Poet He Cannot Read
summary: Dante places Homer at the head of the pagan poets in the Divine Comedy, although he almost certainly could not read the Greek epics directly. His Troy and Homer came largely through Latin authors, summaries, and medieval retellings, especially Virgil. The episode shows how Homer's authority could remain powerful in western Europe even when access to the Greek text was limited.

title: Every Story in the Shadow of Troy
summary: The Iliad and Odyssey became exceptionally influential models for epic, homecoming, war narrative, recognition, and heroic identity. Their reception passed through many intermediaries—Greek education, Virgil, medieval Troy traditions, translation, colonial education, and modern rewriting—and was never confined to a single continuous 'Western' line. Works from Pope and Keats to Joyce, Walcott, and Atwood demonstrate repeated adaptation, while similar narrative patterns also arise independently in other traditions.

title: Ulysses — Homer in Dublin
summary: James Joyce's Ulysses, published on 2 February 1922 and set during one day in Dublin, uses the Odyssey as an elaborate but often ironic framework. Leopold Bloom, Molly Bloom, and Stephen Dedalus are not simple modern equivalents of Odysseus, Penelope, and Telemachus; the parallels organise experiments in style, urban life, sexuality, and identity. Joyce's suppressed episode titles helped readers recognise how an ancient epic could be dismantled and rebuilt inside a modern novel.

title: The Man Who Went to Yugoslavia to Find Homer
summary: Milman Parry developed an account of Homeric formulaic language and travelled to Yugoslavia in 1933–35 to study living South Slavic oral epic. His team recorded thousands of texts and performances, demonstrating that highly skilled singers could compose long songs through inherited formulas and themes. The comparison transformed Homeric studies, though South Slavic practice is evidence by analogy rather than proof of every stage of archaic Greek composition; Parry died in a firearm accident in 1935, and Albert Lord extended the work.

title: The Poems Are More Extraordinary Than We Thought
summary: Parry and Lord established oral-formulaic composition as indispensable to understanding Homer, but scholarship has not concluded that the poems are merely anonymous communal products or that a final shaping poet did not exist. The Iliad and Odyssey can be both traditional and artistically distinctive, with oral performance, textualisation, and later editing interacting in ways that remain debated. The result is a more complex achievement: inherited language and stories organised into monumental poems whose exact route into text cannot be reconstructed.

title: Troy Without Homer
summary: For much of the Latin Middle Ages, direct access to the Greek Iliad and Odyssey was limited, but Troy remained a major literary subject. Latin works attributed to Dares and Dictys claimed eyewitness authority and fed influential retellings by Benoît de Sainte-Maure and Guido delle Colonne, which in turn shaped Chaucer and other writers. These traditions did not simply replace an absent Homer; they created a distinct medieval Troy centred on genealogy, chivalry, romance, and moral history.

title: Schliemann Digs Through Homer's Troy to Find It
summary: Heinrich Schliemann began excavating Hisarlik in the 1870s, helping establish the mound's importance while using methods that destroyed substantial archaeological context. The hoard he called 'Priam's Treasure' came from a level much earlier than the conventional date of the Trojan War, and his staging and removal of it from Ottoman territory remain controversial. Later excavations—not Schliemann alone—showed that Hisarlik contained a long sequence of substantial settlements compatible with ancient Troy, without proving Homer's narrative.
